strengths: First systematic study of safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion-based LLMs, addressing a critical gap for this emerging model class
Well-motivated vulnerability identification grounded in architecture-specific mechanisms (bidirectional modeling + parallel decoding)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 dLLM families and 3 major benchmarks with very strong results (up to 100% keyword-based ASR, 78.5% improvement over baselines)
Thoughtfully designed DIJA framework with multiple diversification strategies (prompt variations, masking patterns, benign separators)
Demonstrated robustness of attacks against existing defense mechanisms, highlighting urgent need for dLLM-specific defenses
Extensive reproducibility details, prompt templates, and ablation studies (generation length, masked token counts)
Clear factorization of vulnerability (Eq. 7) and insightful analysis of why defenses designed for autoregressive models fail
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in attack method itself—interleaved mask-text prompt construction via in-context learning is relatively straightforward; primary contribution is vulnerability identification rather than algorithmic innovation
Absence of white-box attacks (e.g., GCG-based variants); only black-box attacks evaluated, limiting comprehensiveness of threat model analysis
Restricted victim model coverage: only 4 dLLM families (all masked diffusion models), mostly 7-8B parameters; generalizability to other non-autoregressive architectures unclear
Insufficient analysis of solutions—paper identifies vulnerabilities but proposes no defenses; dismisses perplexity-based approaches without deep investigation; limited guidance for practitioners
Evaluation methodology concerns: no human validation, keyword-based ASR is weak metric, no false positive analysis, heavy reliance on GPT-4o as evaluator without assessing evaluation bias
Weak theoretical analysis—while Eq. 7 provides factorization, deeper formal analysis of why interleaving creates exploitability is missing; observations on Figure 6-7 lack theoretical grounding
Limited baseline comparisons: ReNeLLM is strongest baseline but designed for autoregressive models; no baselines adapted specifically for dLLMs
Missing ablations: no statistical significance testing, no human evaluation, no analysis of practical likelihood of such attacks in real deployment scenarios

strengths: First systematic study of safety vulnerabilities in diffusion-based LLMs, addressing an important emerging problem
Clear technical intuition for why dLLMs are vulnerable: bidirectional context modeling and parallel decoding create unique attack surface
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dLLM models, benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), and metrics (ASR-k, ASR-e, HS, SRS)
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over existing methods (100% ASR-k, 78.5% gains on JailbreakBench)
Practical automated attack pipeline using in-context learning without manual prompt engineering
Ablation studies examining generation length and masked token count effects
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of interleaving [MASK] tokens and using LLMs for refinement; lacks novel algorithms or theoretical framework

Overclaimed 'fundamental vulnerability': Figure 3 shows dLLMs have comparable defensibility to autoregressive LLMs against existing attacks, suggesting the vulnerability may be specific to this attack design rather than architectural
Narrow model scope: only 4 dLLMs evaluated, all relatively recent and potentially under-aligned; unclear how findings generalize to other dLLM architectures mentioned only as future work

Insufficient evaluation depth: relies entirely on GPT-4o for evaluation (no human evaluation or inter-rater agreement), limited defense testing (only 2 non-dLLM-specific defenses), no statistical significance testing or error bars
Purely attack-focused with no proposed defenses or constructive solutions; conclusion merely states urgent need for rethinking without guidance

Reproducibility concerns: code availability link incomplete, some implementation details missing or relegated to appendix, sensitivity to hyperparameters (Figure 7) suggests results may not generalize
Unfair baseline comparisons: PAIR and ReNeLLM weren't designed for dLLMs; no adapted versions of existing methods for fair comparison
Shallow technical analysis: claims about parallel decoding preventing intervention lack formal justification; Equation 7 is straightforward without deep insight
Ethical considerations inadequately addressed: no discussion of responsible disclosure with model developers before publication of potentially dangerous techniques
Overstated vulnerability framing: paper doesn't explore whether similar mask-based attacks could work on autoregressive models or whether this is truly unique to dLLMs

strengths: First systematic investigation of safety vulnerabilities in diffusion-based LLMs, identifying a novel architectural weakness specific to bidirectional context modeling and parallel decoding
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 dLLM models, 3 jailbreak benchmarks, and multiple metrics with convincing results (up to 100% ASR-k, 78.5% improvement over baselines)
Clear presentation of the vulnerability with intuitive explanations and concrete examples that effectively communicate why dLLMs are fundamentally vulnerable
Practical and automated attack framework (DIJA) that requires no manual prompt engineering or harmful content obfuscation, using in-context learning for scalability
Strong reproducibility support with promised code release, detailed implementation details in appendix, and comprehensive evaluation metric definitions
Important timeliness: addresses safety of emerging dLLM paradigm before widespread deployment, with clear relevance to AI safety and alignment communities
Robustness analysis including defense mechanism evaluation and impact analysis of masked token numbers and generation length
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in the attack method itself—once the vulnerability is identified, using masks and in-context learning refinement is relatively straightforward; the main contribution is problem identification rather than technical innovation
Missing white-box attack baselines such as GCG, limiting understanding of where DIJA fits in the threat landscape relative to strongest possible attacks on autoregressive models

Minimal exploration of defenses or mitigation strategies; paper identifies vulnerabilities well but offers limited actionable guidance for how to fundamentally redesign dLLM alignment to address this class of attacks

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: limited explanation of why DIJA so dramatically outperforms ReNeLLM (78.5% improvement), missing ablations on prompt template design choices, and disconnected generation length analysis
Limited model coverage with only 4 dLLMs evaluated (all 7-8B parameters), no evaluation of larger models, other architectures, or non-English variants; generalization uncertain
Evaluation metrics rely heavily on GPT-4o which has known consistency issues; no human evaluation provided despite assessing harmful content; StrongREJECT better but still imperfect

Generalization concerns: attack depends on mask tokens (what if dLLMs detect masks?), all prompts from specific benchmarks, refinement models much larger than victims, and uncertainty about robustness to distribution shift
No ablation studies on attack components (prompt diversification, masking patterns, separator insertion) and limited analysis of sensitivity to in-context learning examples

Fairness of comparisons: comparing attack designed specifically for dLLMs against methods designed for autoregressive models is somewhat asymmetric; adapted baselines or defense-specific comparisons would be stronger
Missing responsible disclosure discussion—no indication of whether model developers were notified before publication, which is important for safety research ethics

strengths: First systematic investigation of safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion-based LLMs, identifying architecture-specific weaknesses rooted in bidirectional modeling and parallel decoding
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 victim models, 3 benchmarks, 4 baselines, and multiple metrics with rigorous ablation studies (Table 11) demonstrating the core mechanism
Strong empirical results with up to 100% keyword-based ASR and 78.5% improvement over ReNeLLM, with high stability across runs (std < 0.7%, Table 10)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithms, implementation details, stability analysis, prompt templates, mask syntax mapping, and commitment to code/model release
Rigorous evaluation methodology including human validation of harmfulness scores with >93% inter-rater agreement (Table 18) and multiple evaluation metrics to reduce bias
Thoughtful treatment of threat model assumptions and responsible disclosure practices; proposes preliminary defense strategy (Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment) with targeted evaluation
Clear technical insight into why dLLMs are vulnerable: forced contextual coherence at masked positions fundamentally prevents refusal at inference time
weaknesses: Attack mechanism is relatively straightforward—exploiting an obvious architectural difference; ablation (Table 11) shows 54.8% ASR-e achievable with simple heuristic templates without LLM refinement, limiting novelty
Practical threat model limited for current deployments: closed-source dLLM APIs don't yet expose arbitrary mask placement; threat is prospective, not immediate

Defense solutions are preliminary and incomplete: alignment strategy requires 10k examples specifically for this attack pattern, unclear generalization to novel variations; non-negligible task performance degradation (GPQA: 32.4→27.5); no evaluation against adaptive attacks
Limited scope: exclusively focuses on text-only dLLMs; newer multi-modal models (Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a) unexplored; multi-modal masking may have different safety properties
Section B.6 shows significant performance degradation under UI constraints (single mask span: 31.5% ASR-e), raising questions about real-world applicability when deployments restrict mask usage

Incomplete analysis of existing defenses: paper shows Self-reminder and RPO ineffective but doesn't deeply explain why or explore bidirectional defense strategies; no discussion of system-level detection or monitoring
Evaluation metrics have limitations: keyword-based ASR is crude; human validation on only N=100 samples; no inter-rater disagreement analysis or qualitative failure case examination

Core attack shows straightforward heuristic components (prompt diversification, benign separator insertion) without principled motivation; contribution feels somewhat incremental relative to the vulnerability identification itself

strengths: Identifies a novel and timely vulnerability specific to diffusion-based LLMs' architectural properties before widespread deployment
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models, benchmarks, and baselines with strong reproducibility efforts
Clear explanation of why dLLMs are vulnerable compared to autoregressive models
Honest ablation study (Table 11) showing core vulnerability exists even with simple templates
Proposes and evaluates an architecture-aware defense, demonstrating the vulnerability is not fundamental
High-quality evaluation methodology with human validation of metrics (94% agreement, Table 18)
Extensive appendices and promised code release support reproducibility
weaknesses: Threat model is significantly restrictive: attack requires mask-editing capability unavailable on closed-source APIs; for open-source models, users already have direct control, limiting real-world applicability

Attack method lacks technical novelty: core contribution is observing that simple mask-interleaving works on dLLMs; ablations show 94.5% success with basic templates, making LLM refinement role marginal

Overclaims fundamentality of vulnerability: Table 4 shows it can be mitigated with just 10K fine-tuning examples, contradicting 'fundamental safety concern' framing; suggests problem is fixable through standard alignment rather than architectural
Defense work is preliminary and underdeveloped: only one approach explored, achieves ~76% reduction (not robust), shows some utility degradation, lacks exploration of robust alignment feasibility
Limited technical depth: no formal analysis, bounds, or theoretical framework; Equation 6 is trivial; speculation on mechanisms (e.g., Figure 6 explanation)
Evaluation concerns: GPT-4o used both for refinement (DIJA*) and evaluation creating potential circularity; ASR-k metric is superficial; human validation only on 100 samples
Scope limitations: only 7-8B models tested, instruction-tuned variants only, no scaling analysis, no evaluation of other non-autoregressive architectures
Insufficient ethical justification for code release given preliminary defenses and unclear real-world threat model
Presentation issues: sensationalized title and overclaimed novelty; positioning relative to prefilling attacks (similar threat model) is underdeveloped

strengths: First systematic study of safety vulnerabilities in diffusion-based LLMs, addressing an important gap for an emerging model class
Clear and fundamental architectural insight: bidirectional context modeling forces harmful consistency while parallel decoding prevents dynamic rejection, creating a novel attack surface
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dLLM families (LLaDA, Dream, MMaDA), three benchmarks (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT), and strong baselines (GCG, PAIR, ReNeLLM)

Rigorous methodological evaluation including ablation studies (Table 11) isolating the interleaved structure, reproducibility analysis (Table 10, <0.7% variance), prompt diversity quantification (Table 9), and human validation of metrics (93%+ agreement)
Proposed preliminary defense (Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment) demonstrates the vulnerability is addressable, with substantial improvements (ASR-e: 55.5%→25.0%)
Strong reproducibility support with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, prompt templates, model interfaces, and promises of code/data release
Well-articulated core vulnerability with effective visual illustrations and clear presentation
Timely contribution as dLLMs (Dream, LLaDA) are emerging as practical alternatives to autoregressive models
weaknesses: Threat model requires ability to perform remasking/editing on assistant-side outputs; for closed-source models, needs API support for infilling. This significantly limits practical applicability compared to standard autoregressive jailbreaks

Defense work is preliminary and limited: only one proposed mechanism, only 10k training examples, no data scaling analysis, and significant performance drops on general benchmarks (GPQA: 32.4%→27.5%). No evaluation of aligned models against other attacks (PAIR, ReNeLLM)

Unexplained finding that w/o Refinement LLM achieves 94.5% ASR-e vs 55.5% for full DIJA, suggesting auxiliary LLM contributes minimally. This counterintuitive result deserves deeper investigation and questions whether in-context learning strategy is necessary

Generalization concerns: all evaluated models are 7B-8B with similar masked diffusion architectures; scalability to larger dLLMs and architectural variants unexplored. Attack success depends on auxiliary LLM quality, with sensitivity not thoroughly analyzed

Evaluation relies heavily on keyword-based ASR (acknowledged as problematic), and all metrics depend on single evaluator (GPT-4o), though human validation partially mitigates this. Potential benchmark overlap not discussed

Defense mechanism analysis incomplete: shallow investigation of why standard defenses (Self-reminder, RPO) fail for dLLMs; missing systematic analysis of defense-attack interactions and simpler mitigations (e.g., UI constraints on mask placement)
Critical defense results relegated to appendix (Table 4); main paper focuses primarily on attacks rather than solutions, limiting practical contribution
Disconnection between generation length analysis (Figures 6-7) and main narrative; unclear how insights transfer to masked token effects
